title: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
summary: An eigenvalue satisfies Av=λv for some nonzero v, equivalently det(A-λI)=0. The trace is the sum of the eigenvalues and the determinant is the product, over the complex numbers. Real symmetric matrices are orthogonally diagonalizable; a Jordan block need not be diagonalizable at all.
intuition:
An eigenvector of a square matrix is a nonzero vector that $A$ merely stretches. The stretch factor $\lambda$ is the eigenvalue, and the equation is $Av=\lambda v$ with $v\neq 0$. Rearranged, $(A-\lambda I)v=0$ has a nontrivial solution, so $A-\lambda I$ is singular and $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$. That determinant, as a polynomial in $\lambda$, is the characteristic polynomial. Its roots are the eigenvalues. A real matrix can have complex roots; they are still eigenvalues, and they arrive in conjugate pairs so that the trace and the determinant stay real.

Two symmetric functions of the eigenvalues are visible without finding them. Counting algebraic multiplicity over $\mathbb{C}$, the trace equals the sum of the eigenvalues and the determinant equals the product. For a $2\times 2$ matrix the characteristic polynomial is $\lambda^2-(\mathrm{tr}\,A)\lambda+\det A$, which is the same statement. Multiplicity counts: a double root contributes twice to the sum and is squared in the product.

A real symmetric matrix is the case where the geometry is as good as the algebra. Every eigenvalue is real, eigenvectors from different eigenvalues are orthogonal, and there is an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. In matrix form, $A=Q\Lambda Q^\top$ with $Q$ orthogonal and $\Lambda$ real diagonal. Matrices that are not symmetric need not be diagonalizable at all. The Jordan block $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ has characteristic polynomial $(\lambda-1)^2$ and only one independent eigenvector. Algebraic multiplicity $2$ and geometric multiplicity $1$ cannot be the diagonal of a similar diagonal matrix.

definitions.body: A scalar $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of the square matrix $A$ when $Av=\lambda v$ for some $v\neq 0$. The vector $v$ is an eigenvector. The zero vector is never an eigenvector.
The characteristic polynomial is $\det(A-\lambda I)$. Its roots, counted in $\mathbb{C}$ with algebraic multiplicity, are the eigenvalues.

$A$ is diagonalizable when $A=PDP^{-1}$ for a diagonal matrix $D$. This happens if and only if the eigenvectors include a basis. A real symmetric matrix is always diagonalizable, with $P$ choosable orthogonal.

formulas.name: Eigenvalue
formulas.note: The two sentences are equivalent. The determinant condition is the characteristic equation.

formulas.name: Trace, determinant, and the symmetric case
formulas.note: Sums and products count algebraic multiplicity over $\mathbb{C}$. The factorization $A=Q\Lambda Q^\top$ needs $A$ real symmetric: real eigenvalues and an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors.

properties: $Av=\lambda v$ for some $v\neq 0$ if and only if $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$.
Counting algebraic multiplicity over $\mathbb{C}$, the trace is the sum of the eigenvalues and the determinant is the product.
A real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors: $A=Q\Lambda Q^\top$ with $Q^\top Q=I$ and $\Lambda$ real diagonal.
Eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent. For a real symmetric matrix they can be chosen orthogonal.
Not every square matrix is diagonalizable. The Jordan block $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ has a repeated eigenvalue and only one independent eigenvector.

examples.title: A symmetric $2\times 2$ matrix
examples.prompt: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, find the eigenvalues, check the trace and the determinant, and give an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors.
steps: The characteristic polynomial is $(2-\lambda)^2-1=\lambda^2-4\lambda+3=(\lambda-1)(\lambda-3)$. The eigenvalues are $1$ and $3$.
Their sum is $4$, which is the trace. Their product is $3$, which is $\det A=4-1$. Both counts use algebraic multiplicity; here each root is simple.

For $\lambda=3$, $(A-3I)v=0$ gives $v$ parallel to $(1,1)$. For $\lambda=1$, $v$ is parallel to $(1,-1)$. Normalizing, the columns of $Q=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors, and $A=Q\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}Q^\top$.
examples.answer: The eigenvalues are $3$ and $1$, summing to the trace $4$ and multiplying to the determinant $3$. An orthonormal eigenbasis is $(1,1)^\top/\sqrt{2}$ and $(1,-1)^\top/\sqrt{2}$.

examples.title: A Jordan block that is not diagonalizable
examples.prompt: Let $J=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. Find its eigenvalues, the trace and the determinant, and show that $J$ is not diagonalizable.
steps: $\det(J-\lambda I)=(1-\lambda)^2$, so the only eigenvalue is $1$, with algebraic multiplicity $2$. The trace is $2=1+1$ and the determinant is $1=1\cdot 1$.

$J-I=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ is not the zero matrix, and $(J-I)^2=0$. The equation $(J-I)v=0$ forces the second coordinate of $v$ to be $0$, so every eigenvector is a multiple of $(1,0)^\top$.

The geometric multiplicity is $1$, less than the algebraic multiplicity $2$. If $J$ were diagonalizable, both diagonal entries would be $1$, so $J$ would equal $PIP^{-1}=I$. But $J-I\neq 0$. There is only one independent eigenvector, and $J$ is not diagonalizable.
examples.answer: The eigenvalue $1$ has algebraic multiplicity $2$, the trace is $2$, and the determinant is $1$. There is only one independent eigenvector, so $J$ is not diagonalizable.

traps: Dropping algebraic multiplicity. The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ has trace $2$ and determinant $1$ because the eigenvalue $1$ is counted twice, not because a second different eigenvalue is hiding.

Claiming every real matrix has real eigenvalues, or an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. Both conclusions need symmetry. A rotation by a right angle has characteristic polynomial $\lambda^2+1$ and no real eigenvalue.
Claiming every matrix is diagonalizable. The Jordan block $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ is the standard counterexample: one eigenvector, not two.
Allowing $v=0$ as an eigenvector. The equation $A0=\lambda 0$ is true for every $\lambda$ and says nothing. The characteristic equation is what restricts $\lambda$.
python:
def mul(A, B):
    n = len(B)
    return [[sum(A[i][k] * B[k][j] for k in range(n)) for j in range(len(B[0]))] for i in range(len(A))]

def apply(A, x):
    return [sum(A[i][k] * x[k] for k in range(len(x))) for i in range(len(A))]

A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]
# eigenvalues 3 and 1
assert A[0][0] + A[1][1] == 4
assert A[0][0] * A[1][1] - A[0][1] * A[1][0] == 3
assert apply(A, [1, 1]) == [3, 3]
assert apply(A, [1, -1]) == [1, -1]
J = [[1, 1], [0, 1]]
JmI = [[0, 1], [0, 0]]
assert mul(JmI, JmI) == [[0, 0], [0, 0]]
assert J[0][0] + J[1][1] == 2
assert J[0][0] * J[1][1] - J[0][1] * J[1][0] == 1
print(3)

questions.stem: A scalar $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of a square matrix $A$ when
questions.solution: The answer is **A**. The characteristic equation $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$ is equivalent to the existence of a nonzero $v$ with $Av=\lambda v$. The trace condition and a single equality $\det A=\lambda$ are not the definition. Eigenvalues are defined for square matrices, because $A-\lambda I$ has to be square.

questions.stem: For a real symmetric matrix $A$, which statement is true?
options: The eigenvalues may fail to be real.
$A=Q\Lambda Q^\top$ for an orthogonal $Q$ and a real diagonal $\Lambda$.
Eigenvectors from different eigenvalues cannot be chosen orthogonal.
questions.solution: The answer is **B**. The spectral theorem gives real eigenvalues and an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, written $A=Q\Lambda Q^\top$. Option A fails because symmetry forces the eigenvalues to be real. Option D has the orthogonality backwards: different eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix produce orthogonal eigenvectors. A symmetric matrix need not be a projection.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true?
options: The trace equals the sum of the eigenvalues, counting algebraic multiplicity over $\mathbb{C}$.
The determinant equals the product of the eigenvalues, counting algebraic multiplicity over $\mathbb{C}$.
Every real square matrix is diagonalizable.
A real symmetric matrix has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors.
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, B, and D**. Both the trace identity and the determinant identity count complex roots with algebraic multiplicity. Real symmetric matrices have a full orthonormal eigenbasis. C is false: the Jordan block $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ has only one independent eigenvector.

questions.stem: Let $J=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. Which of the following are true?
options: The only eigenvalue is $1$, with algebraic multiplicity $2$.
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, C, and D**. The characteristic polynomial is $(1-\lambda)^2$. Then $J-I=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ squares to zero and is not zero, so the eigenvalue is repeated and the matrix is not the identity. The trace is $1+1=2$ and the determinant is $1$. There is only the eigenvector direction $(1,0)^\top$, so $J$ is not diagonalizable.

questions.stem: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$. Enter the product of its eigenvalues, counting algebraic multiplicity.
questions.solution: The answer is **3**. The product of the eigenvalues equals $\det A=4-1=3$. Explicitly the characteristic polynomial is $(\lambda-1)(\lambda-3)$, and $1\cdot 3=3$. The sum, which is not asked, is the trace $4$.
